articles.title: Why over two-thirds of Americans say their country is in decline
articles.author: Dante Chinni, Director, American Communities Project, Michigan State University
paras: Inflation is causing real economic pain. Worries about healthcare costs have jumped sharply. And 7 in 10 Americans believe the country is in decline.
That is the landscape for the 2026 midterm election, according to a new survey from the American Communities Project at Michigan State University, which I direct.

The findings, which follow up previous data work the American Communities Project has done in 2023, 2024 and 2025, come from a survey of 2,155 American adults over two weeks in September 2026, conducted by the survey research firm SSRS, using an online panel and telephone, with a margin of error of +/- 2.4 percentage points.
The American Communities Project studies 15 types of communities. Taken as a whole, the national numbers reveal an electorate that is unsettled, gloomy and likely looking for change.
Inflation: Deepening concern

Cost of living is a unifying concern for all Americans. For the past four years, when given a list of 20 issues – including abortion, climate change, gun violence, drug addiction, education, healthcare, housing, immigration and taxes – respondents have consistently reported that inflation is the No. 1 issue in their community.
But the new data shows something more significant. Almost half of Americans, 47%, say they are experiencing real pain from rising prices – a sharp rise from previous years.

In 2023, 2025 and 2026, we asked respondents whether they were experiencing “serious financial problems” due to price increases. In July 2023, 27% answered yes. In 2025, 30% said yes. In 2026, 47% said yes. This significant swing underscores that many Americans across the country are really hurting in this economy.

For some groups, concern about costs reached well above 50%. For those ages 18-29 – members of Gen Z – 61% said they are dealing with serious financial problems because of price increases, the highest percentage among the four generational cohorts, including ages 30-49, 50-64 and 65+.

Cost of living was also a particular concern reported among people of color. Overall, 65% of Hispanics and 63% of Black Americans said they are experiencing serious financial problems because of price increases.
Healthcare: A rising issue
Healthcare emerged as a top issue in our new survey.

In 2025, 20% of respondents said it was a top concern in their community. This year, 30% cited healthcare as a top concern, a 10-point jump. That shift also made healthcare the No. 2 issue in this survey, after inflation.

For some demographic groups, concern about healthcare in their community reached above one-third of respondents. Among those whose income falls between US$75,000 and $99,999, 36% said healthcare is a top issue; among Black Americans, 35% said so.
This tracks with the policy changes and public health challenges since our 2025 survey. Many have lost health insurance, hospitals have closed, and disease outbreaks have affected communities.
It also may be tied to increasing costs overall. The pain people feel from inflation in healthcare can be especially acute because the dollar amounts can be large.
The United States in decline
The 2026 survey data also showed a 15-point jump in the percentage of Americans who agree with the statement: The United States is in decline. The number is at 70% this year, up from 55% in 2025.
In some ways that number makes sense. Consider the other numbers mentioned here – pain from inflation and concerns about healthcare – and the mood of Americans in general.

But there is another important point in the data. That number, 70%, is exactly what it was in 2023, the first year the American Communities Project did a survey. In 2025, the “decline” number dropped to 55%, and that change was largely driven by communities that voted for President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

It was a measure of hope for the future, and it showed in massive improvements in the general hopefulness in communities such as the evangelical hubs, concentrated heavily in the South, rural middle America and the middle suburbs.

The fact that the “decline” number is back to 70% suggests those same Trump-supporting communities have seen their hopes take a hit – and a deeper analysis of the data on the American Communities Project website shows just that.
At the very least, the data suggests a very disillusioned electorate.
Times and attitudes change
It’s important to keep the 2024 election in mind as the 2026 midterm elections near. It’s a sign of how opinions and attitudes can change – and quickly.
The data here represents this moment in time, and it will likely move after November, which is why we will field this same survey again after the new Congress is seated.

On Oct. 26 we released our more detailed community-level findings on the American Communities Project website. This data explores how opinions and attitudes differ depending on where and how people live.
Dante Chinni receives funding from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.
Ari Pinkus receives funding from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.

articles.title: I’ve been talking to MAGA supporters for years, and here’s why some are sticking with Trump — and others are not
articles.author: Alex Hinton, Distinguished Professor of Anthropology; Director, Center for the Study of Genocide and Human Rights, Rutgers University - Newark
paras: President Donald Trump’s approval ratings are cratering. Even his Make America Great Again, or MAGA, diehards have reservations.
This fact was evident to me when I attended MAGA rallies in three states on Oct. 24-25, 2026. One was a Turning Point USA get-out-the-vote event outside Harrisburg, Pennsylvania.

Along with a few dozen America First stalwarts wearing white “America the Beautiful” caps, I sat on a wooden table under a small picnic pavilion listening to speakers such as MAGA activist Scott Presler and Trump-endorsed U.S. Rep. Dan Meuser. Meuser reeled off MAGA talking points, including the supposed threat posed by transgender athletes and bathroom use, immigrant voter fraud and the “billionaire anarchist George Soros.”

Remarkably, the speakers barely mentioned Trump. The audience clapped politely, but the energy was tepid compared to the many MAGA rallies I attended in 2024, when the Pennsylvania landscape was dotted with Trump and MAGA signs. This time I saw none.
The numbers bear out what I observed.

A mid-October 2026 poll found that only a third of U.S. adults approve of the job Trump is doing; 71% feel the country is on the wrong track. The majority of Americans are pessimistic. A growing number worry about government corruption.

There’s the war with Iran that has resulted in U.S. soldiers being killed and wounded. The conflict is costing billions of dollars and spiked the price of gas. But most of all, Trump has lost support on the economy amid growing inflation and an affordability crisis.

Remarkably, despite the headwinds, many of Trump’s MAGA loyalists still back him. This point was underscored by the Harrisburg event I attended as well as Trump’s midterm rallies, where attendees still enthusiastically chant “U.S.A.” and are decked out in red caps and MAGA merch.

I’m an anthropologist who has been studying Trump and his MAGA movement for years. I wrote a newly updated book, “It Can Happen Here,” on Trumpism and U.S. history. I have previously written about why people voted for Trump in 2024.

Based on my research, I see three key reasons some voters still back him. Meuser stressed all three at the Harrisburg rally as he warned of “lunatic” left socialism while extolling the Trump administration’s track record, including the immigration crackdown.
1. Socialist doomsday ‘fear porn’

While nervous about the war and inflation, many Trump supporters respond to fearmongering about “radical left” Democrats, some of whom, Trump contends, want to drive the country off a communist cliff.

If Trump has long harped on this putative radical left danger, his warnings have gained new traction with the visibility of progressive hard-liners like Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and the democratic socialist mayor of New York, Zohran Mamdani.

Beyond the threat of socialism, Trump claims that under Democrats the U.S. would fall back into a “dark age” of economic mayhem, curtailed rights and religious freedoms, rampant crime and imperiled national security. MAGA stalwarts echo his warning of “Doomsday” scenarios.
To underscore this point, Trump and his loyalists are connecting the massive and sometimes destructive protests in France to democratic socialists and the “radical left.”

For example, the White House posted a video on X featuring rioting and arson in France which warns, “Pay attention before it’s too late. This is the future Democrats want for America.” Other Trump supporters warn the unrest illustrates the civilizational threat of immigration and a looming “global Islamic takeover.”
MAGA pundits like Jesse Watters and Greg Gutfeld are encouraging this use of what they call “fear porn” to drive the 2026 midterm vote.
2. Border ‘invasion’ shut down
Trump won in 2024 largely due to two bread-and-butter election issues: the economy and immigration.

While those on the left focus on the abuses of Trump’s immigration agents, many Trump supporters I have spoken to credit him for clamping down on what they view as a Biden-era border “invasion.” It resulted, they claim, in the influx of millions of “illegal aliens,” some dangerous criminals, who have strained U.S. cities and taken jobs from citizens.

These Trump-supporting immigration restrictionists argue that reports of abuses by Immigration and Customs Enforcement are exaggerated and the need for mass deportations is urgent. If anything, some contend that Trump hasn’t done nearly enough in this regard.

MAGA loyalists give Trump higher marks on immigration than any other major issue, which is why the Trump administration foregrounds immigration as one of its top “promises kept.” This is why, in Harrisburg, attendees were told that when they went to knock on doors later in the day, they should mention Trump’s promises kept, including “No. 1, a closed border.” The tax cuts and drop in crime were Nos. 2 and 3.
3. ‘America is winning … bigly!’
Trump supporters feel the economic pinch. Some are unhappy about the war. But, they contend, Trump – who wrote the book “The Art of the Deal” – always has a long-term strategy and winning hand.
Supporters point to Trump’s long and self-described successful business career and note what they perceive as the many successes of Trump’s first term.
And they contend that Trump has already delivered. As pro-Trump radio host Dan O’Donnell recently put it, under Trump “America is winning … bigly.”

Trump’s 2025 “One Big Beautiful Bill” cut taxes and government spending while delivering on campaign promises such as “no tax on tips” or overtime. Meanwhile, crime rates have plummeted, while the stock market has reached new highs.

A White House Jan. 20, 2026, press release – “365 WINS IN 365 DAYS; President Trump’s Return Marks New Era of Success, Prosperity” – lists a win for each day of the second term’s first year, some of which fact-checkers have shown are exaggerated. They range “from negative net migration for the first time in 50 years to the largest homicide drop on record, trillions in reshored investments, peace deals ending multiple wars, record energy production and massive bureaucracy cuts.”
MAGA stalwarts, like Trump, are sharing lists of such accomplishments, including Top 25 lists, to turn out the vote.
Trump’s bad polling numbers, some suggest, are the result of an anti-Trump “fake news” psyop. The reality, they say, is that Trump has launched, as he calls it, the “golden age of America.”
A Trump midterm ‘golden wall’?

Does this hardcore base of Trump voters create a “golden wall” that will head off the major midterm gains many expect Democrats to make? This possibility emerges especially in light of polling that has historically underestimated Trump voter strength.
But from my perspective, probably not.

There are splits in MAGA that I have observed firsthand at MAGA gatherings, such as the Conservative Political Action Conference and Turning Point USA’s AmericaFest. The war in Iran has been at the center of the dispute, with some – including former U.S. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene and commentators Tucker Carlson and Megyn Kelly – condemning what they call an “Israel First” faction for betraying MAGA’s “America First” principles.
In contrast, Democrats appear more energized.

Historically, the opposition party almost always makes gains during midterm elections – especially when there are economic troubles. And some wonder whether Trump supporters will turn out when he isn’t on the ballot.

Given the war and affordability crisis, it seems likely Trump’s “golden wall” of MAGA diehards, like those I saw at the Harrisburg rally, won’t be enough to stave off significant midterm losses, including control of the House of Representatives.
The question then will be what, if anything, Trump and his MAGA supporters will do about it.
Alex Hinton receives funding from the Rutgers-Newark Sheila Y. Oliver Center for Politics and Race in America

articles.title: Private equity is buying up more methadone clinics – access to the lifesaving drug isn’t getting easier
articles.author: Yashaswini Singh, Thomas J. and Alice M. Tisch Assistant Professor of Health Services, Policy and Practice, Brown University
paras: Three times a week, Amber Titus wakes up at 5 a.m. to get ready for the 45-minute drive to the methadone clinic.

Titus, 38, and her husband live with their two young children in Bisbee Junction, Arizona, a rural community near the U.S.-Mexico border. The couple started taking methadone, a medication that treats opioid addiction, in early 2025.
“It’s been a godsend,” she said.
But accessing methadone is not easy. The closest place they can receive treatment is a clinic in Sierra Vista, about 30 miles from their home.
The clinic opens on weekdays at 4:30 a.m. but closes before midday. Titus has to get her methadone dose and arrive at work in Bisbee before her shift starts at 9 a.m.
Arriving just 10 to 15 minutes late for an appointment can mean missing a dose because rules are so strict, she said, even when the clinic is still open.

That’s the routine when they have their own transportation. In August, their car was totaled in a crash. Until they got another one, Titus called Medicaid, her insurance provider, to schedule rides to the clinic.
“They said they’d be at my house at 6 o'clock in the morning,” Titus told The Conversation. The driver was late every day. “I missed my methadone dose for the whole week,” she said.

Nationwide, more than 120 people a day died from opioid overdoses in 2025, according to federal estimates. Methadone is one of the most effective medications for opioid use disorder, cutting the risk of fatal overdose by roughly half. Yet only 22% of people with the disorder ever receive it.

For more than five decades, only specialized, government-approved clinics, known as opioid treatment programs, have dispensed methadone, not regular doctors or pharmacies. Many clinics require patients to show up in person every single day, with average one-way drive times approaching 50 minutes in rural communities.
Today, private equity firms have acquired large shares of the market for methadone clinics, telling lawmakers their capital has expanded treatment and modernized care.

I am a healthcare economist at Brown University who studies how private equity is reshaping American medicine. My recent research on private equity’s growing footprint in addiction treatment, co-authored with researchers from the University of Pittsburgh and RAND, found that despite acquiring over one-third of methadone clinics in the U.S., private equity investments have not expanded methadone availability or the construction of new facilities.

This research has informed federal investigations into the role of private equity in expanding access to medications for addiction treatment. Currently, U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., has an investigation into three of the country’s largest methadone clinic operators, citing concerns that they oppose expanding treatment access for financial reasons rather than patient safety.
Why methadone fits the private equity model
Because methadone is so tightly regulated, opioid treatment programs are, in effect, a government-created monopoly.

In most of the country, if you want methadone, there’s a short list of clinics licensed to give it to you and no other way to get it. Moreover, people with opioid use disorder generally must travel to opioid treatment programs every day, where staff must observe them taking methadone, with strict limits on how much methadone patients can take home and when they can do so.
Take-home methadone varies based on the state, time in treatment and clinician discretion. Only 19% of people who received take-home methadone received three or more days’ supply.

That kind of guaranteed, captive demand is exactly the sort of investment that can be profitable for private equity investors. Whoever controls the clinics in a region controls access to the medication and can set the terms for patients in most need of medication.

Private equity firms have invested more than US$1 trillion in U.S. healthcare over the past two decades, touching everything from fertility clinics to hospice care. Many Americans have never heard the term private equity, but these firms now own more than 400 U.S. hospitals and oversee doctors in more than a quarter of the country’s emergency rooms.

In opioid treatment specifically, firms have used a platform and add-on strategy: buying one large clinic, then steadily acquiring smaller nearby ones, similar to a company quietly buying up every gas station in a county until, years later, one owner controls them all. Individually, each deal looks too small to matter. Collectively, a single firm can end up controlling an entire region’s methadone supply.

To be clear, private investment isn’t inherently harmful. Research shows that in markets where quality is easy to see, competition is robust and there’s no government subsidy – restaurants, for instance – private equity can have neutral or even positive effects. Healthcare has none of those features. Patients often can’t judge provider quality, they rarely pay for care directly, and government programs act as both payer and regulator.
Market share grew, methadone supply didn’t
My research has quantified what actually happened after private equity acquisitions of opioid treatment programs.

Previous research I have done, which my ongoing work builds upon, examined acquisitions from 2011 to 2019 and found that within two years of a private equity firm moving into a county, it typically controlled 67% of the local methadone treatment market – and in more than a quarter of counties, a single firm controlled all of it.

Despite acquiring that much market power, these acquisitions generally do not result in the construction of new methadone clinics or an increase in methadone treatment. Additionally, the data shows that methadone shipments, or what clinics have to dispense to patients, and opioid-related deaths were unchanged during the study period.
In plain terms: Private equity firms haven’t been building new capacity – they’ve been buying up the capacity that already existed.

As of October 2026, there are 1,572 methadone clinics registered with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Nationally, 35% of opioid treatment providers are affiliated with private equity firms, and in 19 states and the District of Columbia more than half have private equity owners.

Montana has four clinics, all owned by Community Medical Services, more commonly known as CMS. The company was operating there before it was acquired by private equity. In North Dakota, CMS owns three of the state’s four methadone clinics. In Arizona, CMS owns the Sierra Vista clinic where Titus gets her methadone.

In 2018, a prospective investor advised shutting down CMS’ Montana and North Dakota clinics as unprofitable. Nick Stavros, CEO of CMS, opted to partner with a different private equity firm to keep the clinics open.
Before private equity investment, CMS had 14 clinics in four states. It now has 79 clinics in 14 states, according to Stavros. The total includes five clinics in prisons and three mobile units.
Unlike the typical private equity investment strategy of acquisitions, a majority of the company’s recent growth – 49 clinics – has come from new sites, he said.
No expansion has taken place in Montana. Building a new clinic costs about $2.5 million, more than many rural areas can support, Stavros said.

Proponents of private equity ownership argue it can help fill gaps left by inadequate public funding for addiction treatment. The strongest evidence in their favor: One study found clinics became significantly more likely to accept Medicare and Medicaid after acquisition, likely because large chains can afford administrative infrastructure that small, independent clinics cannot. That’s a real benefit worth acknowledging.
But look past insurance acceptance and ask whether more people are actually getting – and staying on – treatment, and the picture darkens.

For buprenorphine, a related medication that can be prescribed more broadly than methadone, one study found patient volume at private equity-acquired facilities rose about 22% after acquisition. Similar data for methadone was not available. But the same study found the share of patients who stayed continuously on buprenorphine for 180 days – the national quality benchmark – fell by nearly 8 percentage points. Early discontinuation is one of the strongest predictors of relapse and overdose.
A proposal to expand methadone access

These findings matter beyond academic journals, because they are at the heart of an active policy debate. Congress is weighing the Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act 2.0, which would let regular doctors prescribe methadone and let pharmacies dispense it, breaking the decades-old rule that methadone can be dispensed only at opioid treatment programs.
The Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act was introduced in 2023. After facing opposition, it did not reach a House or Senate vote before the end of the congressional term.

Lawmakers later reintroduced the bill with changes as Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act 2.0, which is currently in consideration by the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees. The committees have not yet scheduled the next step, a markup of the bill, and the current congressional term ends in January 2027.

In an email, U.S. Rep. Donald Norcross, D-N.J., one of the bill’s sponsors, recalled a snowstorm years earlier when he noticed a single track of footprints crossing an otherwise empty street to a methadone clinic.
“I realized that no matter what else is happening in the world,” Norcross said, “some of our neighbors’ lives literally revolve around getting to that building every single day.”

The bill has widespread support from patient advocacy organizations and medical societies. At the same time, a STAT investigation found that the main opposition to the legislation comes from the American Association for the Treatment of Opioid Dependence, AATOD, a major trade group representing methadone clinics. This coalition argues that expanded prescribing and pharmacy dispensing of methadone would increase diversion and overdose risk.

The evidence so far does not support that claim. Moreover, firms that control large shares of their local markets may have a financial incentive to keep new competitors, including doctors and pharmacies, out.

Mark Parrino, AATOD’s president, told The Conversation the trade group opposes the bill for two reasons. First, the bill would let the Health and Human Services secretary determine which additional practitioners are qualified to prescribe methadone for opioid use disorder. Second, it would allow methadone to be dispensed in dispersible tablet as well as liquid form.

Tablets “were definitely” involved in a rise in methadone-related deaths that began around 1999, Parrino said. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and a Food and Drug Administration advisory tied those deaths to methadone prescribed for pain, not addiction treatment.

Stavros, who is AATOD’s Arizona representative, said he did not see the bill as a threat to CMS’ business model, but he cited concerns that removing all regulation too quickly could allow a few bad providers to drive up methadone overdoses and increase stigma against the drug.
“We need to find ways to increase access,” he said. “If somebody would come up with … a slow, gradual transition that led to pharmacy prescribing,” Stavros said he would support it.

Dr. Melody Glenn, associate professor of addiction and emergency medicine at the University of Arizona, previously worked at a methadone clinic in Tucson and supports MOTAA 2.0, though she said the legislation should go further.
“It’s time to remove the regulatory barriers to these lifesaving medications,” Glenn told The Conversation in an email.

The bill would allow doctors specializing in addiction medicine, like her, to prescribe methadone. Glenn said it’s frustrating that such an effective treatment for opioid use disorder exists, yet many people who could benefit never receive it.
“They don’t have to die,” she said.
Bringing private equity deals into view
Two other policy responses are gaining traction.

The first is ownership transparency. Regulators, researchers and patients cannot scrutinize what they cannot see, yet private equity is exempt from the disclosure rules that apply to publicly traded companies.

Indiana, California and Maine have enacted or proposed reform to disclose private equity and management company ownership as a condition of being able to bill Medicare or Medicaid. Vermont passed similar legislation this year, on which I was invited to provide expert testimony.

The second is lowering the reporting threshold for acquiring a healthcare company to make them more visible to agencies enforcing U.S. antitrust laws, which are intended to promote competition and prevent monopolies.

The U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission consider ownership of 30% or more of a local market for a product or service a red flag for anticompetitive behavior. Yet, as my research shows, private equity chains typically control at least 67% of a local methadone market within two years of their first clinic purchase in a county.

The reason most never trigger the federal reporting requirement is because these acquisitions happen through a series of smaller, piecemeal deals rather than one large merger. The reporting requirement applies only to deals worth more than about $134 million. Some states have introduced proposals to lower thresholds to around $10 million specifically for healthcare deals, so the vast majority become visible to enforcement agencies before they close.
Structural barriers to getting treatment

The U.S. is experiencing an ongoing and severe opioid crisis. In 2023, approximately 80% of the more than 100,000 drug overdose deaths involved an opioid. In 2024, federal data shows the number of people who died from drug overdoses declined to nearly 80,000, and more than 54,000 of those deaths involved opioids.

We already have medications that work. The barriers preventing people from accessing them are not primarily clinical. They are structural – and, in this case, actively maintained by financial investors who profit from the status quo.
“Addiction isn’t a choice,” Titus told The Conversation.
She and her husband work for Cochise Harm Reduction, a grassroots nonprofit organization based in rural southeast Arizona that works to make life better for people who use drugs.
“It’s a learning curve and eventually … you get tired of it and you want help.”

Aleka Kroitzsh, researcher, and Kristi Tanner, senior accountability editor, contributed reporting. The author of this article is supported in part by Arnold Ventures, which also provides funding for accountability reporting at The Conversation.

Yashaswini Singh receives research funding from the National Institutes of Health, Arnold Ventures, and the Commonwealth Fund, and serves on the advisory council of the Private Equity Stakeholder Project.

articles.title: Budget 2026: experts on what John Healey’s ‘breathing space’ plan means for households
articles.author: Alper Kara, Head of Department of Economics, Finance & Accounting, Brunel University of London
paras: It was a “breathing space” budget from Chancellor John Healey. In the absence of big surprises or bold change, Healey’s trade-off appears to be small reliefs now in exchange for “fresh hope” in the future. Here’s what our experts made of the chancellor’s first budget.
Targeted help with energy costs as bills keep rising
Jonquil Lowe, Visiting Academic, The Open University

This budget took place against a backdrop of global turmoil and rising inflation, driven largely by higher energy costs. These are continuing to squeeze household budgets. From January, the energy price cap is predicted to rise by 27% to nearly £2,200 a year for a typical household.

Help with energy costs is therefore an important move. This support includes a £100 energy payment for households in England in council tax bands A to D (the devolved governments will receive equivalent funding to replicate this).

There was also a commitment to abolish the standing charge for gas (currently on average 30 pence a day). The amount will instead be added to the charge for the unit cost of each kilowatt-hour used. This gives households more control over their bills – it will mean that limiting the amount of gas they use will have a bigger effect on reducing their cost. However, one worry is that squeezed households could still risk their health by not heating their homes adequately.

Labour’s manifesto pledged not to raise taxes on working people. This budget technically kept to that if we assume that working people just receive earnings. But building on last year’s changes, this budget has introduced another increase to the tax rates on interest from savings and rental income. Landlords and some savers will be taxed at a basic rate of 24% (currently 20%), higher rate 44% (from 40%) and additional rate 49% (from 45%) from April 2027.

This makes it all the more welcome that a proposal last year to cut the cash ISA limit for savers aged under 65 to £12,000 is being abandoned. Everyone, regardless of their age, will still be able to put up to £20,000 a year into a cash ISA (or cash and money funds within a stocks-and-shares ISA) and receive the interest tax-free.

The government will also consult on setting up a first-time buyer ISA to replace the Lifetime ISA and help people save for a home. From February 2027, a new scheme called Your First Home will provide equity loans for first-time buyers purchasing new properties. The loan, worth 20% of the purchase price, will be tax-free for the first five years. To be eligible buyers must have a household income of no more than £110,000 (£140,000 in London).

The budget also delivered a higher tax-free personal allowance for pensioners on the lowest incomes. The new Pension Tax Allowance will be applied automatically, with HMRC doing the sums. Pensioners with income up to £13,037 (the full state pension) will pay no income tax from April 2027. For comparison, for younger people the standard allowance is frozen at £12,570 until April 2031. They would pay £93.40 tax on an income of £13,037.

The announcements come on top of a drip feed of “everyday fixes” in the days leading up to the budget. These included reform of carer’s allowance so that carers no longer lose their whole allowance of £86.45 a week once their earnings pass a weekly limit of £204. But it has already emerged that this much-touted change will not come into effect until 2030 while the government updates its IT systems.
Small clues that this government is chasing growth
Maha Rafi Atal, Adam Smith Senior Lecturer in Political Economy, University of Glasgow

For years, the UK has faced a structural deadlock: a public that demands robust state services, but which rejects both the broad-based income taxes and pro-growth measures like increased immigration that might fund those services. Under Rachel Reeves’ chancellorship, Labour tried to get around this by raising the necessary taxes indirectly – from everywhere but income. This made it more expensive for businesses to operate, failing to jumpstart growth.

In this budget, John Healey has tried a different tack, deploying selective business reliefs alongside a commitment to increased defence spending. Together, these measures make a calculated gamble that state stimulus can rescue the economy from lacklustre growth. In a growing economy, the government gets more tax revenue to fund services even without raising rates, because there’s more economic activity to tax in the first place.

The reliefs for business are welcome. Raising the small business rate relief threshold – effectively removing half of all shops, restaurants and gyms from the rates system – provides breathing room for local economies. When paired with the electricity bill reduction for core industries and the introduction of “founders’ relief” for entrepreneurs selling shares in their business, the budget offers some incentives for corporate investment and entrepreneurial risk.

The chancellor has also listened in part to businesses that complained of rising costs as a result of the increase in employers’ national insurance and the new measures in the Employment Rights Act. While the minimum wage is set to rise, the government has restored a lower rate for younger workers. This will benefit some businesses in employing people more cheaply, but the government also hopes it will help absorb school-leavers and graduates into the workforce, increasing productivity and reducing the welfare bill.

The budget introduces two distinct avenues for the state to proactively stimulate growth. First, through accelerated defence commitments (spending 3% of GDP by 2030, for example), the chancellor is injecting capital directly into domestic supply chains, manufacturing, and high-tech engineering. Second, the roadmap for fiscal devolution offers a regional stimulus by promising to let mayors keep 100% of local business rates by the end of the decade, as well as a share of income tax receipts. This kind of arrangement, to fund infrastructure and attract business, is standard practice in most federalised systems. But its absence has been an unusual quirk of UK devolution.

Yet, while these measures are constructive, it is not clear that they are enough to reverse the grim reality: growth is stagnant at just over 1% and the Office for Budget Responsibility predicts it will stay that way.

Unlike its predecessor, this government seems to accept that it desperately needs some growth, and therefore some private investment, or public services will fall apart. In this budget, it has signaled some understanding that it may have to meet business halfway to get there. But the fiscal forecast relies on the hope that these stimuli will take effect in time to expand the tax base and preserve public spending before the next election.

If they do not, the Treasury has also signaled that like Reeves before him, Healey will resort to spending cuts in the final years of the parliament to balance the books. By deferring that choice, the government has chosen to pray for a growth miracle today, while keeping the threat of real-terms austerity on the horizon tomorrow.
Banks to pay more – but Healey bids to keep them lending
Alper Kara, Professor of Banking and Finance, Brunel University of London

One surprise is the relatively modest increase in taxes on banks compared with what financial markets had been expecting. There had been speculation that the government would raise the surcharge on bank profits from 3% to 8%. Instead, the surcharge will increase to 6% for just 15 months, from January 2027. So banks will face a higher tax bill, but a smaller one than many investors had feared.

Shares in some major UK banks rose as investors welcomed the smaller-than-expected increase. This suggests that investors believe the profitability of banks will be less affected by the tax increase than previously feared.

But the decision also reflects the difficult balance facing the chancellor. The government needs more money to support public spending and manage its finances, particularly at a time when borrowing costs remain high. Banks are an attractive source of revenue because their profits have been relatively strong in recent years.

And since 2023, higher interest rates have helped many banks earn more. These profits come from the difference between what banks charge borrowers and what they pay savers. So, the government has a reasonable argument that banks should make a greater contribution to public finances. This is especially true when households and businesses have been struggling with high living costs.

However, the amount of additional revenue matters. Taxing banks more will generate £1.5 billion in extra income for the Treasury, but it is unlikely to make a substantial difference to the government’s wider spending commitments, such as defence. A temporary increase also means that the additional revenue cannot be relied upon over the longer term.

And the next question is who will ultimately pay for this tax increase. Banks could absorb the additional cost through lower profits and reduced returns to shareholders. Alternatively, they might try to protect their profitability by offering lower savings rates, charging higher interest rates on new mortgages and business loans, or increasing fees for customers.

However, competition in the banking market will limit how much of the tax banks can pass on to customers. Banks that increase mortgage rates or reduce savings rates risk losing customers to competitors. Given that the surcharge increase will last only 15 months, my view is that banks may prefer to absorb much of the additional cost rather than risk losing market share.

The chancellor’s decision to keep the annual cash ISA allowance at £20,000, rather than reducing it to £12,000 as previously planned could also help banks. Cash ISA deposits are an important source of funding for banks and building societies, particularly for mortgage lending.

Keeping the higher allowance could help banks retain those deposits and avoid additional funding pressures. This may also be part of the chancellor’s attempt to balance higher bank taxes with the need to keep banks lending to households and businesses.

There are also wider considerations. Higher taxes could affect the international competitiveness of the UK banking sector, as banks consider taxation when deciding where to expand their operations. Sustained higher taxation could discourage investment in the UK banking sector, potentially leading to fewer new jobs or even job losses over the longer term.

By opting for a smaller and temporary increase, the chancellor appears to have recognised these risks. His decision seems to be aimed at a balance between raising additional revenue and limiting the impact on lending and investment.
Relief on energy bills could remove push for heat pumps
Dylan Ryan, Lecturer in Mechanical & Energy Engineering, Edinburgh Napier University
The overall cost of heating with gas will drop for most people, except for those with larger homes, after the chancellor’s announcement.

Once the standing charge, a fixed daily fee, is removed, gas bills will reflect what people actually use. While these lower-than-expected bills will be a welcome relief for bill payers, it could weaken the economic case for households to switch to using heat pumps.

There had been rumours of cuts to the boiler upgrade scheme intended to help more home owners install heat pumps. However, that didn’t happen. A government report on the scheme said that 65% of property owners who installed heat pumps did so because this grant was available. The report also pointed out that 52% of all recipients of the grant were large detached four-bedroom or bigger homes. So, some sort of reform could be needed.
The cut to VAT on electricity and the £100 paid to those in bands A-D homes will also provide some relief for energy bill-payers.

However, energy prices are expected to rise again by the next price cap adjustment in January 2027, due to the Iran war pushing up global energy prices. The government may need to provide some additional relief then. For example, further decoupling electricity prices from the price of gas, as gas often sets the price for electricity.
Ultimately, moving energy use away from fossil fuels is a balancing act. But the government is going to have to make further changes if it expects to meet its climate change targets by 2050.

The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Autistic children come to A&E in mental health crisis from as young as eight
articles.author: Emma Ashworth, Associate Professor in Child & Adolescent Mental Health, Liverpool John Moores University
paras: Research consistently shows that autistic people face higher risks of mental health difficulties and are more likely to think about or attempt suicide than the general population.

For example, a 2014 study found that up to 66% of those surveyed had had suicidal thoughts (compared to 20% of non-autistic adults) and up to 35% have planned or attempted suicide. There may be many reasons for this, but it is thought that pressures such as chronic stress, isolation and bullying, compounded by trauma, anxiety and inadequate support, can lead to exhaustion and hopelessness.
We need to find ways to intervene earlier with autistic young people, to build wellbeing, prevent crisis and create safer environments around them.

To help us do this, we need to look at the experiences of autistic children across education, health and social care services. This includes A&E, where past studies have shown that autistic children are nine times more likely to receive psychiatric care than non-autistic children.

Our study – a collaboration between researchers at Liverpool John Moores University, children’s mental health charity Anna Freud, Edge Hill University, University College London and Alder Hey Children’s NHS Foundation Trust – set out to map patterns among young people in suicidal crisis at A&E. We analysed the records of 338 young people aged eight to 16 who attended a UK paediatric hospital A&E for suicidal crisis over three years.
Patterns within emergency departments

We found that autistic young people were disproportionately represented, at over a third (35.8%) of all attendees. Nearly two thirds of these (62%) were girls. This mirrors the way autistic girls are often under-identified in childhood, leading to missed or late diagnosis and more internalising difficulties. This can result in an increased risk of anxiety, depression and suicidality.

The data showed autistic children were seeking help for suicidal thoughts in A&E at significantly younger ages than their non-autistic peers (eight v ten years). This could suggest that the cumulative emotional toll of negative experiences builds up faster or starts earlier for autistic children. It’s consistent with previous research which found that negative school experiences generate twice the emotional burden in autistic and ADHD adolescents compared to their neurotypical classmates.

We found that autistic young people were more likely to have a pre-existing mental health diagnosis (64% v 46%). They were also more likely to have previously been seen by Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS)(74% v 49%) and to have repeat A&E attendances for suicidal crisis (31% v 18%).

This highlights a paradox: autistic young people were more likely to be known to CAMHS and to have sought help at A&E previously, but were also more likely than non-autistic young people to attend (and re-attend) A&E in suicidal crisis. This points to a gap between recognising an autistic child is struggling and delivering the help they need, with A&E departments left to act as a safety net when earlier support falls short.

As this was a single-site UK study based on routine clinical records (which can be incomplete), we may not be able to generalise the findings to other settings. Despite this, we think these findings have implications for how to provide earlier and better care.

CAMHS are incredibly stretched. Limited resources means the threshold to receive help is very high, with many not getting support as a result. Barriers are even steeper for autistic young people. For example, “diagnostic overshadowing”, where symptoms of mental health difficulties are attributed to autism, is common. Furthermore, some therapeutic options aren’t suited to how autistic people think and communicate. Improving the accessibility of services and offering adapted support could help reduce the risk of crisis.

Alternatives to A&E are also needed. The government’s recent announcement of 159 new NHS mental health centres in England will help provide crisis care in the community. However, crisis alternatives tailored to the needs of autistic people still need to be developed and delivered, to offer more appropriate pathways specifically for autistic young people. Improved early intervention in schools and communities can also support prevention.

The A&E environment is likely also part of the problem, with bright lights, noise and unpredictability intensifying overwhelm. This can make it harder to assess a young autistic person and more likely they’ll leave before being seen. Small changes like quiet rooms and ear defenders could help.

Communication differences can further complicate A&E experiences for autistic people. Expressing distress non-verbally may increase the risk of crisis being misread, missed or misunderstood, particularly in such a busy environment. Tools like communication passports and reasonable-adjustment flags are starting to appear in some NHS services but could be made standard practice.

These changes are not possible without services being given adequate funding and resources. Staff training in autism is also key, with the NHS-funded National Autism Trainer Programme providing a good model.

Our findings show that something isn’t working in services for a group of children at serious risk of harm. In collaboration with autistic young people and their families, we need to turn this evidence into action, providing much earlier support and building safer, more understanding environments so that no one falls through the gaps.
Emma Ashworth received funding from Liverpool John Moores University QR Policy Support Fund to conduct the research associated with this article.
Georgia Pavlopoulou has an honorary contract with mental health charity Anna Freud. She is Chair of Autism Central, England's Autism Peer Education Programme.

articles.title: Punishment alone won’t help gang-involved teens – a former child soldier explains why
articles.author: Charles Wratto, Non-Resident Research Fellow, Igbinedion University Okada
paras: When Americans hear of child soldiers, they may imagine tragic images of children wielding rifles on distant battlefields.
But the conditions that help warlords recruit children into armed conflict abroad also help gang leaders draw young people into violent organizations in the U.S.

In cities across the country, gang violence continues to claim lives and fracture communities. A September 2025 FBI report recorded 69,273 incidents involving gang activity – most often assaults – between 2021 and 2024. Young people ages 13 to 16 were the most frequently reported offenders.
Policy responses to this crisis have largely focused on policing, prosecution and tougher penalties. Those responses cost federal, state and local governments billions of dollars annually.
Far less attention is paid to why violence offers some young people a sense of purpose, belonging and identity in the first place.

Gang-involved youth in the U.S. are not child soldiers in a legal or conventional sense, and American gangs are not rebel or insurgent groups. Nonetheless, the ways some young Americans become embedded in violent organizations – and the difficulty of leaving them – overlap remarkably with the child soldier experience.

As a former child soldier who is now a peace and conflict studies researcher, I have lived through organized violence and have since studied how violence shapes young people’s relationships, identities and opportunities. This work has led me to ask how decades of research on child soldier recruitment and reintegration might help young Americans caught in gang violence.
Recruitment is not always coercion

Research on child recruitment – and my own peacebuilding work, including negotiating the release of abducted children in Mali, South Sudan and northern Nigeria – shows that children are not always forced into armed groups at gunpoint. Their pathways into such groups cannot be understood as the result of coercion alone.

Armed groups may reach children through peers, community networks, relatives or other social connections. In places marked by insecurity and limited opportunities, children may not make a single decision to enter violence. Rather, relationships and constrained choices can draw them closer until entry seems like a viable way to gain a perceived sense of security and control over their own lives.

In many American cities, gang involvement follows a similar path: A 2025 study of 1,808 male adolescents in Multnomah County, Oregon, who have been referred to the juvenile justice system, found that exposure to gang-involved peers and relatives was associated with a greater likelihood of gang membership.

Through social networks, as well as music and online culture, gangs can project status, power and recognition. For young people who feel excluded by peers or disconnected in school, or who face instability at home, these signals can make gang involvement appear to offer something immediate and tangible: safety, identity and belonging. Researchers have found that some young people also join partly for protection, even though gang members face a higher risk of victimization than their peers.

Social media has intensified these dynamics, spreading images of violence, wealth, weapons and notoriety far beyond the neighborhoods and front lines where gangs and armed groups operate. The conflict in Sudan offers a stark example: Young fighters have been publicly celebrated and stylized online, including in videos portraying youngsters in military uniform as heroic “lion cubs” and in AI-generated clips placing them beside senior commanders.
Young people in both gangs and armed groups may feel a sense of safety, connection and recognition. But what a young person sees as belonging can become a powerful mechanism of control.

Gang leaders in urban communities, like warlords in conflict zones, often position themselves as providers, protectors, mentors and father figures. They impose rules, settle disputes, reward loyalty and regulate access to opportunity and protection. For marginalized youth, they offer recognition where there is isolation, structure where there is instability and identity where there is exclusion.
That world gives young people purpose and belonging, but both are conditional on loyalty, obedience and participation, which makes leaving difficult even when the risks of staying become clear.
Why punishment alone falls short
Arrests and incarceration can interrupt violence, but they do not necessarily dismantle the systems that draw young people into gangs.

As in conflict settings – where removing children from armed groups does not eliminate commanders, recruiters, networks or incentives – incarcerating young Americans can remove participants from the street without disrupting the structures, relationships or conditions that lured them to gang involvement. When they are released, those same influences may remain, making a return more likely.

This does not mean that young offenders should not be held accountable for violent acts they commit. But evidence from juveniles convicted of serious offenses, including felonies, suggests that punishment beyond what is necessary for public safety does not produce greater deterrence. Young people are rarely the architects of the systems that exploit them. When accountability is directed primarily at the young person at the bottom of that structure, the organization itself can remain intact.

Global prosecutions for child soldier recruitment have largely focused on commanders who direct and exploit children. Likewise, reducing youth violence requires attention to those who organize it, not only those caught in it. If a gang’s leadership, or the networks that profit from it, remain in place, billions spent deterring young offenders will not protect American streets or the children who walk them.
One of the hardest lessons from helping child soldiers return to their communities is that leaving violence does not mean the transition is complete.

Children who leave armed groups are often disarmed, demobilized and provided with vocational training, education and material assistance. But training someone to make a living is different from creating the conditions – a functioning market, infrastructure, mentorship and networks – in which that person can succeed.

For example, when a young person sells the sewing machine or other equipment that a reintegration program gave them to earn a living, it can look like a personal failure. But if the economic environment is unfavorable, or the infrastructure and support systems needed to sustain that new livelihood are absent, those shortcomings may explain the outcome as much as individual decisions do.

A 16-year study in Mozambique found that long-term reintegration of ex-child soldiers was shaped by livelihoods, sustained support, forgiveness and community acceptance. This has a direct lesson for the U.S.: A young person can leave a gang or come home from incarceration and return to a society that primarily sees them as an offender.

A 2021 study conducted across 12 U.S. states found that people with juvenile records face significant barriers to education, credentialing and meaningful employment. Another study found that a juvenile record can hurt an applicant’s employment opportunities.
If the neighborhood, family and institutions around that young person have not changed, the conditions that made violence attractive remain, and stigma can become a mechanism of re-recruitment.
The U.S. does not need to replicate child soldier reintegration programs, but it can learn from their successes and failures.

Removing young people from violent organizations is only part of the solution. The real measure of success is whether there are legitimate alternatives to the social world that violence provides and whether society can hold young people accountable while still creating pathways for them to build new lives.
Charles Wratto is affiliated with the Center for Peace and Violence Prevention (CPVP).

articles.title: Why your vote for local chief prosecutor will matter on Election Day
articles.author: Ronald Wright, Professor of Criminal Law, Wake Forest University
paras: Before most Americans step into the voting booth in November, they will already know their choices at the top of the ballot, in races for governor, the Senate and House of Representatives. But a race near the bottom of the ballot – for the chief prosecutor in their local district – will probably affect the voters’ lives more directly.
As a former prosecutor and as a scholar of the criminal courts for over three decades, I have seen how local district attorneys take the lead in responding to crime. This vote matters.

The chief prosecutor in local criminal courts – the titles vary, such as district attorney, prosecuting attorney, state’s attorney or county attorney – has enormous discretionary power over criminal law enforcement.

While state legislators pass the statutes that define crimes, local prosecutors decide where to spend limited enforcement dollars. They decide which cases to file and work with the police to address the crimes that matter most in each county.
Prosecutors also choose how to negotiate guilty pleas. While judges select criminal sentences in each case, prosecutors influence that choice with their own recommended sentence.
No official matters more than the chief prosecutor when it comes to using the resources of the courts and prisons.
Until the early 2010s, party labels did not matter in these local races, because Republicans and Democrats backed similar priorities. Prison was the central tool at every prosecutor’s disposal.

The prosecutor’s job centered on charging as many people as possible with crimes that could result in the longest possible prison term. Convictions for less serious crimes were valuable ways to build the defendant’s criminal record, making it easy to obtain prison sentences in the future.

Democratic and Republican candidates figured that voters wanted them to be “tough on crime.” Because the easiest way to send that signal was to press for more prisons, the size and cost of prisons mushroomed for decades.
And because most prosecutors presented the same basic options to voters, incumbents usually ran unopposed. Even when opposed, they beat the challengers in most races.
Over the past 10 to 15 years, however, prosecutor candidates have offered voters some real choices.

In King County, Washington, for example, voters in 2022 chose a candidate who emphasized prevention and mental health services alongside traditional criminal prosecutions. Her opponent had instead promised to file more criminal cases.

Voters today have more power to decide how many jail cells they want to fund and use. More traditional prosecutor candidates might continue to focus on prisons in their responses to crime, relying on its presumed power to incapacitate criminals.

This was the campaign strategy of a 2025 challenger in Norfolk, Virginia, who called for a return to heavier prison use after four years of efforts by the incumbent to reduce incarceration. Voters rejected this proposal and returned the incumbent to office.

Reform-oriented prosecutors, such as the district attorney in Milwaukee, are depending on less expensive nonprison punishments, including treatment programs for a wider range of crimes, reserving prison for more serious violent offenses. These reordered priorities seem to work as designed. They reduce prison use without increasing crime rates.

These reform-oriented prosecutors, like the county attorney in Minneapolis, might also develop diversion programs, sending some defendants into community service programs. Typically, prosecutors offer diversion to defendants under age 18. Some offices, such as the Pima County attorney in Arizona, offer diversion to adults accused of less serious crimes.
Some prosecutors, like the district attorney in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, design and lead some of these programs themselves. Often they partner with nonprofit groups that promote public safety.

Prosecutor candidates also give voters choices on which defendants to hold in the local jail, at public expense, while their charges are pending. Some offices have reduced or eliminated the use of cash bail, without increasing local crime. Candidates also give voters choices about new approaches to victim support services and programs designed to improve the reentry of convicted people into the community.

Apart from the various options that prosecutor candidates can offer, voters can expect prosecutors to work transparently. Candidates can commit to routinely releasing data about office operations. That’s what the Democratic candidate did in her successful race for commonwealth attorney in Arlington, Virginia. That data can allow journalists and researchers to evaluate trends over time, not just information about individual cases.

There are many offices – such as Jacksonville, Florida, and Boulder, Colorado – that show their work on data dashboards. That transparency allows the public to judge, between elections, how well the prosecutor delivers on campaign promises.

Recent political trends show that prosecutor elections are becoming more competitive, with more incumbents facing challengers. These races are also being driven by politics at the national level, as voters increasingly elect prosecutor candidates from the same party they prefer in national and state offices.
In this changing environment, I believe it’s worth voters’ time to explore expanded options in prosecutor races.

articles.title: What legal experts say about the Trump administration’s attempts to make a federal case out of state elections
articles.author: Naomi Schalit, Politics and Legal Affairs Editor, The Conversation
paras: The Trump administration’s lawsuit against Alaska, which seeks to block certification of the U.S. Senate results there if the GOP candidate does not win, is the latest in a long series of actions throughout 2026 in which the administration has attempted to wrest control of federal elections from states.

In the Alaska case, the U.S. Department of Justice, directed by President Donald Trump, claims that it aims to “protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska.” If incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan does not win reelection in a close vote, the DOJ asserts, it’s likely the result of voter confusion because another candidate with a very similar name – Daniel J. Sullivan, with no party affiliation – is on the ballot, too. So in the event that Sen. Sullivan fails to win reelection, the DOJ demands that Alaska not certify the election and instead should conduct an inquest into who voters thought they were voting for.

The campaign of the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, whose potential win in the hotly contested election could help shift the Senate to Democratic control, has called the lawsuit “wholly baseless” and “an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections” in a court filing. Another filing states that the DOJ lawsuit “asks the Court to preemptively nullify Alaska’s U.S. Senate election and disenfranchise Alaska voters without any legal basis whatsoever. It seeks to go where law ends.”

There’s lots of other heated language in the case’s legal filings. But colorful language and legal citations are a much longer way of articulating a simple fact: The U.S. Constitution gives the president no authority over federal elections. That authority rests with the states and, to a limited degree, with Congress.
Over the past year, as the 2026 midterm elections approached, The Conversation has published a number of stories illustrating this fundamental constitutional rule. Here is a selection of them:
1. The Constitution bars presidential control

“States are empowered under Article 1, Section 4, of the Constitution to conduct elections and set the time, place and manner of those elections,” former federal judge John E. Jones told The Conversation in an interview on April 22, 2026. Jones was discussing Trump’s March 31 executive order to take control of mail-in voting from states and give it to the U.S. Postal Service and the Department of Homeland Security.
Jones, who is now the president of Dickinson College, explained why the framers of the Constitution set up a process in which states run elections and not the federal government:

“First of all, the federal government didn’t have the apparatus to conduct elections. And states had been running elections; they knew how to do it. There was a great deal of trust in the states’ ability to run elections. And there was the core debate of federalism, as to what powers states could retain, and they didn’t want to abdicate many of those powers,” Jones said.

There was also, Jones added, “a debate about the potential for fraud, that if there was a single entity controlling all the elections – that is, if you centralize elections under one politically motivated executive – it’s a really fraught situation which can be abused.”

“The Constitution is clear,” said Jones. “Unless amended, Article 1, Section 4 is – to use the trite phrase – what it is. The power rests with the states, absent congressional action. There is no mention of the president. None.”
2. Limits on Congress, too
The Republican-controlled House also tried this year to horn in on the constitutional power of states to regulate elections and who can vote.

In February 2026, the House, urged by Trump, passed the SAVE America Act. The act would have required those registering to vote in federal elections to – in person – “provide documentary proof of U.S. citizenship.” It also required some people who were voting in federal elections to give proof of U.S. citizenship.

John J. Martin, an election law scholar at Quinnipiac University Law School, wrote that the act “presents a constitutional dilemma. By requiring individuals to show documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to vote, the SAVE America Act is implicitly saying that someone must be a U.S. citizen to vote in federal elections.”

In other words, Martin wrote, “Congress would be instituting a qualification to vote, a power that the Constitution leaves exclusively to the states. Normally, when state and federal laws conflict, the Constitution’s supremacy clause mandates that federal law prevails. Yet, in this instance, where Congress has no actual authority to implement voter qualifications, the SAVE America Act would seem to have no constitutional leg on which to stand.”
The Senate proved unwilling to pass the SAVE Act this year, so this particular constitutional battle has yet to hit the courts.
3. A bar on federal limits to mail voting – so far

Trump frequently targets mail voting, claiming it’s rife with fraud. The March 2026 executive order by the president aimed, it said, to ensure “integrity in federal elections” by placing severe restrictions on mail voting.

Among that order’s provisions was a directive to the U.S. Postal Service to implement, election scholar Martin wrote, “uniform ballot and envelope requirements for mail and absentee ballots used in federal elections.” The order also mandated that states must “provide the Postal Service, 60 days prior to Election Day, with lists of all voters eligible to vote by mail or absentee.”

A mail ballot that didn’t comply with the Postal Service’s requirements, or was sent by somebody not on a state-provided list, would not be delivered by the Postal Service, wrote Martin, “effectively canceling that vote.”
Lawsuits were filed by a host of state officials and voting rights groups. The suits eventually made their way up to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Martin summarized their arguments: “The president does not possess unilateral authority to alter the methods of voting in federal elections. Rather, the elections clause of the Constitution vests the authority to regulate the ‘time, place, and manner’ of federal elections in the states. Congress also has the authority to regulate federal elections, if it chooses to do so.”
On Sept. 14, 2026, the Supreme Court apparently agreed, with a 7-2 vote upholding a preliminary injunction blocking the new rules.

articles.title: Data centers are inspiring bipartisanship – for now
articles.author: Barbara A. Trish, Professor of Political Science, Grinnell College
paras: It may not be as shocking as rogue AI agents hacking another system, but the current political resistance to data centers has taken a surprising turn: It’s bringing together strange bedfellows, from democratic socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders to right-wing strategist Steve Bannon.

Organized opposition to new data centers, made up of a coalition of varied interests, has spread across the nation. Through protests, packed zoning commission meetings, moratoriums and other government action, the resistance has upended dozens of proposed projects.

Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. They’re also massive facilities that require extraordinary amounts of energy. By 2030, U.S. data center electricity use is expected to reach 12% of the nation’s total consumption.

They carry some benefits. At the national level, data centers fuel the computing power seen as critical to U.S. competition with China. Locally, they create an uptick in jobs, especially during the construction phase, and can generate tax revenue. In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, though, the heavy costs associated with them – such as land use, higher household utility bills and environmental degradation – appear to outweigh the benefits, bringing together people who usually find themselves politically at odds.

I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of AI in political campaigns is reshaping established practices and power dynamics. I believe data centers may be disrupting some of the partisan issue alignments Americans have grown to expect.
Political disruption – AI style

Despite ongoing debate about the extent of and reasons for polarization, one thing is for sure: Democrats and Republicans stake out distinct positions on many issues. Pew Research Center data shows, for example, that 63% of Democrats say climate change is a very big problem facing the country, compared with 14% of Republicans, a 49-point gap.

By contrast, the partisan gap on data centers is small – and getting smaller: In summer 2026, the Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans whether they support the construction of data centers in their communities. Supporters of both parties were more opposed than supportive, although opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%. That partisan gap had narrowed over the previous four months, moving from 18 to 15 points.

This year has been marked by considerable upheaval: political, economic and technological. Americans have been hit hard with surging fuel and energy prices. And with rapid AI development, they witness real-world examples of the sort of lapses in safety that have worried both AI insiders and observers.

One “rogue” attack announced in July 2026 involved OpenAI’s AI agents escaping a secure environment and autonomously – without human direction or assistance – breaking into the system of Hugging Face, another AI company. Shortly after, news broke that out-of-control AI agents were not just a one-off limited to that hack.

Polling shows that majorities of both parties feel that AI technology is developing too fast, though Democrats’ levels of concern are 22 points higher than Republicans’. The gap is much smaller – 4 points – on support for government keeping AI under human control and on protecting U.S. workers. Backing for each is very high, hovering around 80%.

This bipartisanship on attitudes about AI and data centers appears also to show up in alliances on the ground and, in some cases, in new organizations with a focus on thwarting data centers. For example, New York’s No Data Center FLX has organized protests, sued the local zoning board of appeals and collected almost 23,000 petition signatures in opposition to a proposed data center.

Government makes decisions about data centers at all levels. In cities and counties, zoning fights draw a disparate resistance: environmentalists, folks reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests.

Some bipartisanship has extended to Congress. In mid-September, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a wide margin: 417-3. The bill requires states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs.

The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill, which would establish a voluntary structure, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers. Comparable sentiment killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change.

As midterm elections approach, candidates up and down the ballot are blanketing the airwaves and digital channels with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump, for his part, has weighed in, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.” It’s a fine line for some Republican candidates between responding to voter concerns and not alienating the president.

If data center politics seem familiar, it may be because this isn’t the first issue to bring together such a diverse coalition: In the 1990s, opposition to the North American Free Trade Agreement did the same, uniting organized labor and environmentalists, frequent adversaries, over concerns about job losses and pollution. That alliance never extended beyond the boundaries of its singular focus on trade agreements, though. Similarly, don’t expect data centers to permanently reshape the U.S. political landscape.
